standard.title: Daily life continuity and change
standard.description: continuity and change between aspects of their daily lives and their parents' and grandparents' childhoods
standard.prior_knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFK02): Students explored celebrations and commemorations and their significance. From AC9HS1K01: Students compared family structures and roles across generations.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify continuity and change between aspects of their daily lives and their parents' and grandparents' childhoods.

nodes.label: Aspects of daily life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify key aspects of daily life (home, family traditions, leisure, school, shopping) and describe what these look like today.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three aspects of daily life (e.g. toys, school, home) and describe what they look like today.
nodes.typical_width: Explore a range of aspects of daily life including homes, family traditions, religious and cultural practices, leisure, school life, rules and consumer habits; describe each aspect using concrete examples from their own experience.
wider: Examine traditional toys and games used by First Nations Australian children, such as Arrernte string games, and discuss their purpose in cultural learning
Explore daily life aspects for children in another country today and compare with Australian daily life
nodes.hinge_reason: Students need a clear contemporary baseline for each aspect of daily life before they can meaningfully compare with the past — comparison requires knowing what 'now' looks like.

response_modes.reason: Build a class inventory of contemporary daily life aspects using personal experience, photographs and objects before introducing historical sources for comparison.

success_criteria: Identifies at least three aspects of daily life from their own experience
Describes what each aspect looks like today with a concrete example

nodes.label: Comparing past and present daily life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare aspects of their daily life with the same aspects in their parents' or grandparents' childhoods, identifying similarities and differences using sources.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two aspects of daily life between their childhood and a grandparent's or parent's childhood, identifying one similarity and one difference.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and comment on photographs and oral histories to find out how daily lives have changed and remained the same across generations; compare homes, toys, school, leisure and cultural practices.
wider: Compare daily life across three generations (grandparents, parents, self) and track a pattern of change over time
Use artefacts and photographs to compare daily life in two different cultural contexts from the same time period

response_modes.reason: Oral histories and photographs from family members are the richest source — the range of comparison cases in the class creates natural breadth.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Generational comparison within diverse families — especially where grandparents grew up in different countries or cultural contexts — produces rich, authentic historical comparison.
success_criteria: Compares at least two aspects of daily life across generations
Identifies at least one change and one continuity between past and present daily life

nodes.label: Using comparative language for change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use comparative language to describe change and continuity across generations, applying terms from provided vocabulary.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least three comparative terms (e.g. 'bigger than', 'more rainy', 'fewer') accurately when comparing past and present aspects of daily life.
nodes.typical_width: Apply comparative language when describing family life over time: 'smaller/bigger', 'closer/further', 'hotter/colder', 'fewer/less', 'younger/older'; use these terms accurately in written and spoken responses.
wider: Create a comparison chart or Venn diagram showing daily life changes and continuities, labelling with comparative language
Identify which changes were the most significant and give a reason for their choice

response_modes.reason: Comparative language requires accurate usage — practise through categorisation tasks, sentence frames and labelling before expecting fluency in extended writing or discussion.

success_criteria: Uses at least three comparative terms accurately when describing change over time
Comparative language is applied to specific evidence, not used generically
